title: When a Spring Boot service handles a request, how much memory does that single request actually consume? Break down the sources: the thread stack, the request and response objects, JSON buffers: and explain how you measure per-request overhead in production using heap diffs, Actuator, and AOP.
shortTitle: Per-request memory overhead in Spring Boot?
keyPoints: Thread stack reserves 512 KB to 1 MB of native memory per worker thread, controlled by -Xss.
The deserialized request object graph (DTO, entities, collections) lives on the heap until the request ends.
JSON serialization buffers peak at roughly twice the response payload because the object graph and bytes coexist.
200 Tomcat threads at 1 MB each reserve about 200 MB of stack before a single request arrives.
Heap-diff measurement forces GC, runs N requests, forces GC again, and divides the difference by N.
Actuator plus Micrometer exposes allocation rate, which divided by throughput gives bytes allocated per request.
AOP around-advice on controllers samples per-endpoint heap delta for attribution.

s1_definition.oneliner: One Spring Boot request costs a thread stack plus its object graph plus about twice the JSON payload, and you measure it with heap diffs, Actuator metrics, and AOP sampling.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Thread stack** – each Tomcat worker thread reserves native memory (commonly 512 KB to 1 MB via `-Xss`), attributed to the request occupying that thread.
- **Request object graph** – Jackson deserializes the JSON body into a DTO, which lives on the heap until the request completes.
- **Business-logic objects** – entities loaded from the database, intermediate collections, mapping DTOs, and stream pipelines.
- **JSON serialization buffers** – the response object graph and its serialized byte form coexist during writing, peaking at roughly twice the response payload.
- **Measurement** – heap diffs give rough retained bytes per request, Actuator plus Micrometer gives allocation rate, and AOP around-advice gives per-endpoint attribution.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of one request as one customer walking into National Bank of India. The customer needs a desk reserved the moment they enter (the thread stack), a copy of their filled-in form (the request object), the papers the teller pulls and scratch calculations (domain objects and collections), and a printed receipt plus the carbon copy made while printing (the JSON buffers, which briefly need twice the paper). If you want to know how much paper and desk space one customer costs, you count the supplies before and after serving a thousand customers and divide, you watch the branch's live supply meter (Actuator), and you station an observer at the door who notes supplies used per customer (AOP).

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a Spring Boot service handles a request in the classic thread-per-request model, that single request consumes memory from four main sources. First is the worker thread's stack, which is native memory reserved when the thread is created and is commonly around one megabyte, so a pool of two hundred Tomcat threads reserves roughly two hundred megabytes before a single request even arrives. Second is the deserialized request object graph that Jackson builds from the JSON body. Third is everything the business logic allocates while processing, which for a report endpoint can dominate everything else. Fourth is JSON serialization, where the object graph and the growing byte buffer coexist, so the transient peak is roughly twice the response payload.

At National Bank of India our statement endpoint loaded every transaction for an account into memory and serialized a large JSON response, and that doubling during serialization, combined with no pagination, drove long garbage-collection pauses under load. The lesson was to paginate and to stream large responses so no single request ever holds a huge object graph.

To measure per-request overhead I use three complementary techniques. The heap-diff method is the most direct: force a garbage collection, read used heap, run a known number of identical requests, force GC again, read used heap, and divide. In production I rely on Actuator and Micrometer, dividing allocation rate by throughput. For per-endpoint attribution I add an AOP aspect that samples heap before and after each controller call.

The important nuance is that per-request measurement is inherently noisy because many requests run concurrently and garbage collection is asynchronous. The trustworthy signals are allocation rate and retained heap under steady load.

Remember one sentence: one request costs a thread stack plus its object graph plus about twice the JSON payload, and you measure it with heap diffs, Actuator, and AOP.
